sources.citation: Verstraete, Jean-Christophe. 2026. Prestopped nasals in Umbuygamu (Morrobolam): from prestopping to preaspiration. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56(e2): 1-29. doi:10.1017/S0025100325100807 (CC BY-NC-ND).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Instrumental study of prestopped nasals, not of stress; treats stress as given: 'root-initial consonants were weakened and lost, stress shifted to the second syllable' (p.6); compounding 'characterized by shift of primary stress to the stress position of the second root and loss of the initial vowel of the first root' (fn.4); transcriptions mark stress on the vowel after the first consonant ([aˈpmal] 'foot', [iˈtna] 'ear', [ˈt̪uɸu] 'palm cycad'); prestopped nasals sit in 'the onset of the stressed syllable (due to shift of stress)'.
sources.locator: sec. 2.2 p.6 (historical stress shift), fn.4 p.6 and sec. 5.2 (compound stress shift), sec. 6 p.~25

sources.quote: 'the stress pattern of roots differs depending on whether they are vowel- or consonant-initial: vowel-initial roots have stress on the second syllable, as in (24) [/aˈran̪/ arranh 'nest'], while consonant-initial roots have stress on the first syllable, as in (25)' (p.257); 'compound structures are defined by a distinct stress pattern, with stress falling on the stressable syllable of the second root' (p.258); 'Given that roots only allow second-syllable stress for vowel-initial forms, any consonant-initial forms with stress beyond the first syllable should be analysable as compounds ... (32)
sources.locator: section 'Stress and word structure', pp.257-259 (pdf pp.13-15); examples (24)-(32)
sources.note: Dedicated JIPA Illustration with an explicit stress section (pp.257-259) by the language's principal modern describer; should replace/join the 1994 MA sub-thesis as deciding source. downloaded now; confirms V-initial -> 2nd syllable, C-initial -> 1st, compound stress on 2nd root, residue = historical compounds.
